# Durable Objects Rules & Best Practices

Choose one object per entity that needs coordinated state. Keep essential data in durable storage; in-memory state must be reconstructible. Prefer SQLite for new classes, and inspect the backend of existing classes before selecting APIs. For idle WebSocket servers, prefer hibernation and plan for state restoration.

Fetch the relevant current documentation before implementing or reviewing changes.

| Task | Documentation |
|------|---------------|
| Choose object boundaries, deterministic routing, parent-child relationships, or initialization | [Rules of Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/rules-of-durable-objects/index.md) |
| Choose SQLite or maintain an existing KV-backed class | [SQLite storage API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/index.md); [Legacy KV storage API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/legacy-kv-storage-api/index.md) |
| Review storage gates, external I/O races, transactions, or schema initialization | [Rules of Durable Objects](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/rules-of-durable-objects/index.md); [SQLite storage API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/sqlite-storage-api/index.md); [Durable Object State](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/state/index.md) |
| Configure class lifecycle changes | [Class exports](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/durable-objects-migrations/index.md); [Legacy class migrations](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/durable-object-class-migrations-legacy/index.md) |
| Set placement hints or jurisdiction constraints | [Data location](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/reference/data-location/index.md) |
| Create stubs, invoke RPC, or use HTTP handlers | [Invoke methods](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/create-durable-object-stubs-and-send-requests/index.md); [Namespace API](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/namespace/index.md) |
| Schedule per-object work and handle retries | [Alarms](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/api/alarms/index.md) |
| Restore WebSocket connection state after hibernation | [Use WebSockets](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/websockets/index.md) |
| Handle exceptions, restarts, and shutdowns | [Error handling](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/best-practices/error-handling/index.md); [Object lifecycle](https://developers.cloudflare.com/durable-objects/concepts/durable-object-lifecycle/index.md) |

For verification, use [Testing Durable Objects](testing.md). Keep API signatures, configuration, limits, and implementation examples in the linked docs.

## Alarm-handling review of `Room`

**1. `setTimeout` is used where an alarm is needed (the main bug).**
- A Durable Object can be evicted or restarted at any time, and the timer is in-memory only, so it is lost when that happens. Nothing then triggers `flush()` except the `alarm()` handler.
- Your code never calls `setAlarm()`, so `alarm()` never fires. The hour-long timer also keeps the object pinned in memory while it waits.
- It is also set on every request, so you accumulate one timer per call.

Fix: remove the `setTimeout` and schedule an alarm, only if none exists yet:
```ts
if ((await this.ctx.storage.getAlarm()) === null) {
  await this.ctx.storage.setAlarm(Date.now() + 60 * 60 * 1000);
}
```
`setAlarm()` replaces any existing alarm and there is one alarm per object. The `getAlarm()` guard stops every request from pushing the deadline back, so the flush happens one hour after the first write.

**2. `flush()` ignores the result of `fetch` and can lose or resend data.**
- `fetch` does not throw on 4xx/5xx responses. `alarm()` therefore succeeds even when the sink rejected the payload, and no retry happens.
- Nothing clears `pending` after a successful send, so the next flush resends the same data.
- If the sink is down, `fetch` throws. Alarms retry automatically with backoff, but only when `alarm()` throws.

Fix:
```ts
async flush() {
  const pending = (await this.ctx.storage.get<string[]>("pending")) ?? [];
  if (pending.length === 0) return;
  const res = await fetch("https://example.com/sink", {
    method: "POST",
    body: JSON.stringify(pending),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`sink ${res.status}`); // triggers alarm retry
  await this.ctx.storage.delete("pending");
}
```
Because alarm delivery is at-least-once, a retry after a partial failure can send a batch twice. Include a batch ID or idempotency key so the sink can de-duplicate. Also, `pending` may be undefined, and your code would POST `"undefined"`.

**3. Writes during the `fetch` can be lost.**
Requests can add to `pending` while `flush()` awaits the network call. Deleting the whole key afterwards would drop those items. Snapshot the item count (or IDs) before sending, and remove only those entries afterwards. Using a SQL table with row IDs makes this simple.

**4. No rescheduling after a successful flush.**
If more work has arrived, `alarm()` should call `setAlarm()` again. Otherwise the next flush only happens after another request sets one.

**5. Smaller points.**
- `count` is a read-modify-write. It is safe here because the object has no `await` between the get and put that yields to other requests, but a single synchronous SQL statement or an in-memory counter persisted on write is cleaner.
- The skill's guidance prefers RPC methods over `fetch()` and SQLite-backed storage (`new_sqlite_classes` in migrations) for new classes. That is optional for this fix.
- Add the generic type (`DurableObject<Env>`) and a constructor if you need `env`.

I read the durable-objects skill and its rules reference, and reviewed your class against them. No Cloudflare API tools applied, so nothing was called or changed.
